# Numerical Optimization & Linear Algebra — exam-eve notes

*typed at 1am, 9am exam. only wrote what i half-remember, sorry future me. abbrevs: gd = gradient descent, f' = derivative, grad = gradient vector, H = Hessian.*

## 1. Gradient Descent (GD, "steepest descent")

idea: grad f points UPHILL, so walk opposite it. update rule: x_{k+1} = x_k − alpha · grad f(x_k). alpha = step size / learning rate. if alpha too big → oscillate then diverge (saw it blow up in tutorial); too small → crawls. stop when ||grad|| ~ 0. for convex f this converges to the global min (proof was lecture 4, not in these notes). every lecture sheet calls it "gd", prof writes eta for alpha.

### GD tiny numerical example (tutorial 3, this one is solid)

f(x) = x^2, so grad = 2x, start x0 = 4, alpha = 0.1:
x1 = 4 − 0.1·(2·4) = 4 − 0.8 = 3.2
x2 = 3.2 − 0.1·6.4 = 2.56
x3 = 2.56 − 0.512 = 2.048
pattern: each step multiplies error by 0.8 (= 1 − 2·alpha), linear convergence, marches down to the min at 0. with alpha = 0.3 the factor is 0.4 and it hits 1.6, 0.64, 0.256 — same rule, shrinks faster. don't push alpha past 1 for this f or the factor flips past −1 and it diverges past the min. prof loves asking "what does alpha control" — tradeoff between step length and speed; too big overshoots past the min every iteration instead of shrinking toward it.

## 2. Newton's Method (Newton–Raphson)

for solving f(x) = 0: linearize at x_k, i.e. f(x_k) + f'(x_k)(x − x_k) = 0, solve that line for where it crosses zero: x_{k+1} = x_k − f(x_k)/f'(x_k). geometrically: the tangent at x_k is the line y = f(x_k) + f'(x_k)(x − x_k); set y = 0, solve, that's the next x. repeat. converges QUADRATICALLY near a simple root — error constant e_{k+1} ≈ [f''(x*)/(2f'(x*))]·e_k^2, so right digits double each step — massively faster than gd, but only LOCAL: bad x0 → jumps to another root or blows up. breaks when f'(x_k) = 0 (divide by it). standard way to get sqrt's: f(x) = x^2 − a.

### newton for MINIMIZATION — attempted derivation (INCOMPLETE!!)

want grad f(x) = 0, so run Newton–Raphson on g(x) = grad f(x). Jacobian of g is the Hessian H(x_k) (entries H_ij = d^2f / dx_i dx_j). so:
x_{k+1} = x_k − H(x_k)^{−1} · grad f(x_k).
scalar sanity check: f = x^2, H = 2, grad = 2x → x − 2x/2 = 0, lands on the min in one step, neat.
BUT inverting a full n×n H every single step is total pain for big n. so the trick must be to keep some M_k ≈ H^{−1} cheaply and only UPDATE it each step using the new s_k ... where do i even start — THAT'S WHERE I GOT STUCK. ask Arav before the exam, this is definitely 10 marks.

## 3. Line search (Armijo condition) — one thing i copied off slide 14

choose t_k so we don't overshoot: sufficient decrease rule f(x_k + t·d_k) ≤ f(x_k) + c·t·grad f(x_k)^T d_k with c = 1e-4, start at t = 1 and backtrack t → t/2 until it holds (a.k.a. backtracking line search).

## 4. Quasi-Newton methods / BFGS (formula paste — zero intuition written, missed the lecture)

the BFGS update (inverse-Hessian version, straight off the slide):
H_{k+1} = (I − rho_k · s_k y_k^T) H_k (I − rho_k · y_k s_k^T) + rho_k · s_k s_k^T,   rho_k = 1/(y_k^T s_k),   s_k = x_{k+1} − x_k,   y_k = g_{k+1} − g_k where g = grad f.
start with H_0 = I presumably. DFP is "similar, terms swapped" — did not check. y^T s > 0 supposedly keeps H "positive definite" so directions stay descent?? none of this is explained anywhere in my notes, just the formula.

*that's all i have. unit 2 matrices chapter i literally did not open — will lose marks, whatever.*

syllabus.raw:
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Gradient descent
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Newton's method
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Line search (Armijo condition)
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Quasi-Newton methods (BFGS)
Unit 2 (Linear Algebra): Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization
Unit 2 (Linear Algebra): Conjugate gradient method

lesson.oneLiner: Newton's method solves f(x) = 0 (or grad f = 0) by replacing f with its tangent line at each step and jumping to that line's root: x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k).
lesson.why: Gradient descent only knows the slope at one point, so it creeps. Newton also uses curvature, so correct digits double each step near the root. Your notes have the derivation but stop before any numbers, so here is one, computed.
lesson.analogy: Blindfolded gd feels the slope and shuffles; Newton looks at the whole tangent line under its feet and leaps to where that line says zero is.

steps.text: Linearize f at x_k: the tangent line is f(x_k) + f'(x_k)(x - x_k).
Solve the tangent for its root: x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k)/f'(x_k).
Repeat until |f(x_k)| or the step size is below tolerance.
For minimization apply it to g = grad f; the Jacobian of g is the Hessian H(x_k), giving x_{k+1} = x_k - H(x_k)^{-1} grad f(x_k).
Near a simple root the error obeys e_{k+1} = C * e_k^2 (C = f''/2f' at the root), so convergence is quadratic.

pitfalls.text: The update divides by f'(x_k); a zero slope (or singular Hessian) breaks the step.
Convergence is only local: a bad x0 can jump to another root or blow up.
In n dimensions you re-invert an n x n Hessian every step. Your notes call this 'total pain' and stop. BFGS is the fix.
Far from the root, undamped Newton overshoots; practitioners damp it with a line search.

notesGaps: The derivation is cut off mid-sentence: M_k as a cheap H^{-1} update is started but never finished (that is the quasi-Newton idea).
No worked numerical example of Newton anywhere in the notes; the exam will ask for exactly that.
The notes never state a stopping rule or how many digits the answer has.

trace.title: Newton on f(x) = x^2 - 2 (a square root), start x0 = 1.5

result.answer: sqrt(2) = 1.4142 to 4 decimals; Newton's quadratic convergence gets there by k = 2.

narration: Row 0: starting at x = 1.5, f is 0.25 with slope 3, so the tangent lands us at 1.4167.
Row 1: at 1.4167 the residual drops to 0.0069 and one more tangent gives 1.4142.
Row 2: now the residual rounds to 0, and the update from 1.4142 changes nothing visible.
Row 3: x stays 1.4142 with residual 0, so we have reached the fixed point.
Row 4: repeating 1.4142 confirms the iteration has fully locked on.
trace.takeaway: Digits roughly double per step: by k = 2 the table already agrees on 1.4142.

lesson.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[start x0] --> B[compute f and f-prime]
  B --> C[x = x - f divided by f-prime]
  C --> D{f small?}
  D -- no --> B
  D -- yes --> E[return x]

examQuestion.q: State the Newton-Raphson iteration and apply it to f(x) = x^2 - 2 starting from x0 = 1.5 to give sqrt(2) correct to 4 decimals.

lesson.oneLiner: BFGS is Newton for minimization with the expensive part faked: instead of inverting the Hessian each step it keeps H_k ~ (inverse Hessian) and updates it with the rank-two BFGS formula from the last step's s_k and y_k.
lesson.why: Newton's x_{k+1} = x_k - H^{-1} grad f is fast but every step needs a fresh n x n inverse, which your unfinished derivation flagged as 'total pain'. BFGS is literally how that sentence ends: the pasted formula in section 4 of your notes is this update.
lesson.analogy: Learning a door's weight by feel: each push (s_k) and response (y_k) teaches the hinge model another bit, so you never need the spec sheet (the real Hessian).

steps.text: Start from x_0 with the inverse-Hessian guess H_0 = I.
Take the direction d_k = -H_k * grad f(x_k); a positive-definite H_k makes it descent.
Pick the step t_k by line search, e.g. the Armijo backtracking rule in your notes (exact minimizer on a quadratic).
From the new point form s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k and y_k = g_{k+1} - g_k (g = grad f).
Update H_{k+1} with the BFGS formula using rho_k = 1/(y_k^T s_k).

pitfalls.text: If y_k^T s_k is not positive the update loses positive definiteness and d_k can stop pointing downhill.
H_k approximates the INVERSE Hessian (the slide's version); the other form updates H ~ curvature and reads 'terms swapped' - that is DFP, check before quoting.
Without a decent line search the curvature condition fails and BFGS blows up; superlinear convergence is not automatic.

notesGaps: Zero intuition in the notes: nothing says H_k stands in for the inverse Hessian or why that keeps Newton's speed.
s_k and y_k are pasted with no meaning (step and gradient change) and no link to the secant equation from section 2.
No worked example, and no statement of superlinear convergence.

trace.title: Two BFGS steps on f(x) = x1^2 + x2^2/2 - 2 x1 - x2 (min at (1, 1))

result.answer: BFGS with exact line search hits the minimizer x = (1, 1) of f = x1^2 + x2^2/2 - 2 x1 - x2 after only 2 updates.

narration: Row 0: at (0, 0) the gradient is (-2, -1); with H = (1, 0, 1) the direction is (2, 1) and exact line search steps t = 0.5556.
Row 1: from (1.1111, 0.5556) the gradient (0.2222, -0.4444) times the updated H = (0.5062, -0.0247, 1.0988) bends the direction to (-0.1235, 0.4938) and t = 0.9.
Row 2: x lands exactly on (1, 1), the gradient is (0, 0), and H has settled at (0.5, 0, 1) - the inverse of the quadratic's matrix, never computed directly.
trace.takeaway: Two updates, two dimensions, exact minimum: on quadratics BFGS rebuilds the inverse Hessian (0.5, 0, 1) as well as Newton would.

lesson.diagramMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[start x0, H = I] --> B[d = -H times grad]
  B --> C[line search t]
  C --> D[update x]
  D --> E[BFGS update H from s and y]
  E --> F{grad small?}
  F -- no --> B
  F -- yes --> G[done]

examQuestion.q: Write the BFGS inverse-Hessian update, define s_k and y_k, and state why H_0 = I plus two updates solve any 2 x 2 quadratic exactly.
examQuestion.modelAnswer: H_{k+1} = (I - rho_k s_k y_k^T) H_k (I - rho_k y_k s_k^T) + rho_k s_k s_k^T, rho_k = 1/(y_k^T s_k), s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k, y_k = g_{k+1} - g_k. On a quadratic, exact line search makes each update satisfy the secant equation H_{k+1} y_k = s_k; after n = 2 independent steps H spans the whole curvature, so x_2 is the minimizer (trace: (1, 1) with gradient (0, 0)).

lesson.oneLiner: Gram-Schmidt turns independent vectors into an orthogonal set by subtracting, one vector at a time, its projections onto everything kept so far, then normalizes to get an orthonormal set.
lesson.why: It is the hand-computation route to an orthonormal basis and QR factorization, used for least squares and subspace geometry. Your notes do not cover Unit 2 at all, so every line here is added by Vertex.
lesson.analogy: Picking ingredients for a tasting menu: each new one keeps only the flavour no earlier ingredient already brought, so nothing is a repeat.

steps.text: Keep the first vector: u_1 = v_1; normalize to q_1 = u_1 / |u_1|.
For each later vector subtract its projections onto every q kept so far: u_k = v_k - sum_j (v_k . q_j) q_j.
Normalize each u_k to get q_k.
Stop when all input vectors are processed; q_1..q_k is orthonormal and spans the same subspace.
Stack the q's as columns of Q (and the coefficients as R) to get the QR factorization.

pitfalls.text: A vector already in the span of the others gives u_k = (0, 0); normalizing would divide by zero - the input was dependent.
Classical Gram-Schmidt loses orthogonality in floating point; the modified version subtracts each piece immediately and is more stable.
It is a cleanup of a basis, not an eigenvalue method - do not confuse it with diagonalization.

notesGaps: Nothing about Gram-Schmidt, orthogonalization or QR is in the notes at all (Unit 2 was never opened).
No worked projection example to copy the mechanics from.
The link from this process to least squares, which examiners love, is missing too.

trace.title: Gram-Schmidt on v1 = (1, 1), v2 = (2, 1)

result.answer: q1 = (0.7071, 0.7071), q2 = (0.7071, -0.7071); q1 dot q2 = 0, so the pair is orthonormal.

narration: Row 1: v1 = (1, 1) has nothing to remove yet (projection (0, 0)), so u1 = (1, 1) and normalizing gives q1 = (0.7071, 0.7071).
Row 2: for v2 = (2, 1) we subtract the projection (1.5, 1.5) along the first direction, leaving u2 = (0.5, -0.5), which normalizes to q2 = (0.7071, -0.7071).
trace.takeaway: Two vectors in, two perpendicular unit vectors out: q1 . q2 is exactly 0 and both lengths are 1.

examQuestion.q: Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to v1 = (1, 1) and v2 = (2, 1); give the orthogonal vectors and the orthonormal pair, verifying orthogonality.
